teaser: Nine years old, hands behind her back, and not the least bit shy in front of Klimt.
review_notes:
Opening interprets 'first audience' as the sitter and her family. Mäda's later recollections (trips to Vienna for sittings over several months, Klimt being very kind, asking her to hold still a little longer) are paraphrased from interviews she gave late in life: check wording.
Mäda Primavesi: born 1903, died 2000; emigrated to Canada, where she ran a home for convalescent children.
Often described as Klimt's only commissioned portrait of a child.
The dress is said to have been made for the sitting, possibly by Emilie Flöge's fashion salon: stated cautiously.
Provenance: later owned by Jenny Steiner, seized in 1938, returned to the family after the war, given to the Met in 1964 by her daughter Clara Mertens and André Mertens.
Size approx. 150 x 110 cm.

lesson.text: The first person to judge this portrait was its model, and she was nine. Decades later, Mäda Primavesi still remembered the sittings: train trips to Vienna with her parents, months of posing, and a painter she described as very kind, who only asked her to hold still a little longer whenever she got restless.

Her parents were the other first viewers, and they were delighted enough to order a second Klimt right away, a portrait of her mother Eugenia. Otto Primavesi was a banker from Moravia, in today's Czech Republic, and one of the most generous art patrons of his time.

Otto Primavesi poured so much money into the Wiener Werkstätte, the Viennese design workshop that made furniture, fabrics and jewelry, that he ended up running it. The company's losses helped ruin him in the 1920s.

A rich man's daughter in 1912 was usually painted sitting sweetly, with a doll or a pet, looking a bit like a porcelain figure. Klimt filled sheet after sheet with pencil sketches, trying her seated, standing, turned to the side. Then he settled on something much bolder.
See how the pose is built before you look at the face.

lines.label: A solid triangle
lines.text: Feet planted wide apart, head at the top: her body makes a tall triangle, the most stable shape there is. She stands like someone who will not be moved.

lines.label: The band of roses
lines.text: One arm is bent with a hand on the hip, the other disappears behind her back. A garland of fat painted roses runs across her chest and ties the two arms together.

lines.label: Wall meets floor
lines.text: The purple wall stops just below the middle of the picture. Everything under this line is floor, tilted up toward you like a map, so her feet seem to hover on it.

lesson.text: That stance is closer to a little general than to a doll. Klimt usually painted grown women dissolving into ornament, half hidden by pattern. Here the pattern stays behind and under the child, and she stands clear of it.
Klimt treats a nine-year-old the way portraits usually treat adults: frontal, full length, looking straight back at you.

There is no gold anywhere on this canvas. By 1912 Klimt had left his golden years behind. He had seen bright new French painting and switched to pure color laid on in quick, separate strokes. The lilac wall, the white dress, the pink and green floor are all built that way.

The white dress was reportedly made especially for the portrait. Klimt cared about clothes: his lifelong companion Emilie Flöge ran one of Vienna's most fashionable dressmaking salons, and he designed loose dresses for it himself.
The dress and the wall are easy to take in. The floor is a different matter. It is a carpet or a garden, Klimt does not say which, and it is inhabited.

spots.title: The stare
spots.text: Dark eyes look directly at you, level and serious, above a small closed red mouth. No smile for the painter. Her cheeks carry two quick patches of pink.

spots.title: The bow
spots.text: A big blue-and-white ribbon sits in her brown hair. It is one of the few childish things in the picture, painted in a few swirling strokes.

spots.title: Hand on hip
spots.text: Her right arm bends sharply outward, the hand vanishing at her waist. It is a grown-up, slightly impatient gesture.

spots.title: A bird
spots.text: Near her left leg a spotted bird with orange legs stands beside blue and purple blots. Klimt sketches it as loosely as a child's drawing.

spots.title: A fish
spots.text: A purple fish with a yellow head swims across the pale floor. So is this a carpet, a pond or a daydream? The picture keeps all three possible.

spots.title: A pink creature
spots.text: A small pinkish animal, perhaps a little dog, trots above a blue patch. The floor is a playground of toys and pets drawn in paint.

spots.title: Blue waves
spots.text: Along the bottom runs a border of blue zigzags, like water drawn by a child. Her pale shoes step right onto it.

spots.title: Signature
spots.text: GUSTAV KLIMT in small green capitals, stacked on two lines, placed quietly on the floor at the right.

lesson.text: So the playful part of childhood has slipped down into the floor, while the girl above it keeps her dignity. Klimt gives her both: the fish and birds of a child's imagination, and the upright pose of a person to be taken seriously.

The picture's own life was less calm. After the Primavesi fortune collapsed it was sold to a Viennese collector, Jenny Steiner. In 1938 the Nazis seized her property, the portrait included. Her family recovered it after the war.
Mäda Primavesi outlived almost everyone connected to Klimt's Vienna. She moved to Canada, ran a home for children recovering from illness, and died in 2000, at about ninety-six.

In 1964 Jenny Steiner's daughter gave the painting to the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York. Visitors there still meet the same level stare the painter met in 1912, from a girl who had been asked, kindly, to stand still just a little longer.

quiz.question: How old was Mäda when Klimt painted her?
quiz.explanation: She was nine when the portrait was painted in 1912.

quiz.question: What shape does her wide-legged stance form?
quiz.explanation: Feet apart and head at the top make a tall, stable triangle.

quiz.question: What is missing from this Klimt compared with his most famous works?
quiz.explanation: By 1912 he had left gold behind for pure color in quick strokes.

quiz.question: Which animals can you find on the floor around her?
quiz.explanation: A spotted bird and a purple fish appear on the pale floor.

quiz.question: What did her father Otto Primavesi support with his money?
quiz.explanation: He financed the Wiener Werkstätte so heavily that he ended up running it.

quiz.question: Where is the portrait today?
options: The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
quiz.explanation: It was given to the Met in 1964.

facts.text: Klimt chose the pose on the first try, without any sketches.
facts.explanation: He filled many sheets with pencil sketches, trying different poses.

facts.text: Mäda Primavesi lived until the year 2000.
facts.explanation: She emigrated to Canada and died there in 2000.

facts.text: In the portrait, Mäda smiles shyly and looks away.
facts.explanation: She looks straight at the viewer with a serious, closed mouth.
